doc.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012

title: Teaching, stride students and a clinic in Australia
summary: He has taught stride students and given clinics; in Australia he showed children that changing a song is improvising.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you do any private teaching?
See I never took any piano lessons so I don’t think I have the right to rap anybody’s knuckles. But yes, I mean — what, tell me?
Well, you have something, I’m sure, that a lot of piano teachers don’t have — practical experience in how to play what your ear is telling you and all that kind of stuff. And that’s valuable.

If anything — and I have had a number of students over the years, some stride students who want to learn how to do that because it’s just something that’s so old that very few people do it anymore. Although there’s a wave of young players coming up right now who are fascinating for that very reason. It’s something that’s so old that they’re listening to really old scratchy recordings and saying oh this is great, and learning it from the sheet © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

as well. And sometimes the sheet music doesn’t capture what the live recording does, the groove, the bounce. So if I have students, and every once in a while I’ll do some clinics overseas and in colleges. And I love it. Because people are surprised at how much they know already. In other words, I remember in Australia talking to some kids and I brought them all on stage. I got there an hour and a half before the show and I said, “How many chairs can we fit on stage?” We brought all the chairs up on stage so they could actually — I took the top off the piano so they could see all the internal mechanisms, and they liked that. And I played something for them and it was a Christmas carol that had some Australian words so it’s sort of the Jingle bells/Batman smells/Robin laid an egg sort of thing. But in Australia “Doggie in the boot” and “tuscayute” and all these Australian slang things. And they loved that. And I said, “How many times have you listened to your — it’s not a walkman it’s an iPad, and you heard a note or a word that you changed to your own. And you changed something — it wasn’t Lady Gaga’s, it wasn’t 50 Cent or somebody’s. And oh they unanimously agreed, yes I’ve changed some of these. Well you’re improvising. I said, “The fancy word to describe that is ‘improvising.’” They were making something up that wasn’t there before. “You are doing a variation on something that was already there.” And I said, “If you can do that, it’s a very small step to improvising everything.”
